extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers / experimental scientists / empirical investigators
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on experimental/inductive methods for discovering and testing natures in natural philosophy (Francis Bacon's taxonomy of 'instances' for reasoning about nature). Covers kinds of experimental instances to use, how to design discriminating tests, and cautions about artifacts. Intended as methodological rules for empirical investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instances of the cross
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances used to decide between two competing accounts of a nature by producing an experiment or observation that would occur under one account but not the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct experiments that would distinguish alternative causes (i.e., produce contrary-predictive outcomes). Examples given: (a) look for comets that do not follow diurnal motion to test whether heavenly bodies have different poles; (b) test whether gravity is attraction by placing identical clocks at high and low positions to see if weight-driven clocks slow at height and speed up below (greater or lesser power of weights); (c) magnetic polarity: put a magnet under a pivoted needle to see whether needle retains magnet-imposed poles or returns to terrestrial poles when removed; (d) test whether moon’s light implies solidity by trying to observe reflection from rare bodies (flame, clouds); (e) projectile motion: discriminate between 'air carries projectiles' vs. 'internal parts propel themselves' with experiments like bent reeds or split pens that spring forward; (f) gunpowder explosions: discriminate expansion-of-flame-only accounts versus violent escape/expansion of crude spirit (nitre) by comparing with more inflammable or flame-repelling substances; (g) flame's transitory nature: enclose one flame within another to see whether a flame persists when not compressed by air. Use such cross-instances to allow or disallow hypotheses. Note: cross-instances can show possibility or cast suspicion but may not be final proof; design must ensure the alternative causes lead to distinguishable outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instances of divorce
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances that show the separation of a nature from the concrete substance with which it is usually found; they demonstrate that associated natures can be dissociated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use divorce-instances to expose false generalizations and to show that commonly paired qualities are not inseparable. Examples: heat, light, rarity, and mobility are often associated yet can be separated (air is rare and mobile but not hot or light; moon is light but not hot; boiling water is warm but not light). Magnetic action is offered as an instance where natural action and corporeal substance are divorced (action exists across space), which can be used to argue that natural power may not require a corporeal medium and thus supports consideration of incorporeal substances. Instances of divorce do not decide causes but indicate separability and counter-examples to hasty theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instances of the lamp (immediate information) — five classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances that assist the senses and thereby provide immediate, trustworthy information from which to build understanding; divided into five kinds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The five classes are: (1) strengthen, enlarge, and correct immediate operations of the senses; (2) reduce matters beyond the senses into the sphere of the senses; (3) indicate continued processes or series only seen at their ends; (4) supply the absolute wants of the senses; (5) excite attention and observation while limiting undue subtilty. Seek abundant and accurate 'lamp' instances because interpretation starts from the senses and progresses to understanding; each class has its own experimental methods (see separate rubrics for the 'door/gate' and 'citing' subclasses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Instances of the door or gate (assists the senses, esp. sight)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances (instruments or aids) that enable the senses to perceive what they otherwise cannot: to perceive objects not naturally seen, to see from greater distance, or to see more accurately and distinctly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Threefold assistance to sight: (a) perceive otherwise invisible minutiae (microscope) — reveals hidden form/motion but is limited to very small objects and may not scale to larger objects; (b) view distant objects (telescope) — reveals stellar structure (Milky Way composed of small stars), moons of Jupiter, lunar surface irregularities, sunspots, etc., but telescopic 'demonstrations' should be treated with caution when evidence is sparse; (c) correct and guide sight with measuring devices (measuring-rods, astrolabes). Use such 'door' instances to extend and correct sensory input; be aware of limitations and scope of each instrument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citing / invoking instances (reduction to the sphere of the senses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances and methods that reduce objects or actions that escape direct perception into forms the senses can apprehend, by substitution, surface indicators, instrumental mediation, or artful separation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify why an object escapes the senses (distance, interposition, small quantity, insensible time-scale, excessive velocity or slowness, overwhelming impression, senses already occupied) and choose a reduction method accordingly: (a) substitute a perceptible sign for distant objects (fires, bells); (b) use surface or outward effects to infer interior states (pulse, urine for bodily state); (c) make invisible 'spirits' manifest by their effects (rust, desiccation, softening/melting from retained spirit); (d) use instruments (thermometer) to render expansions/contractions visible; (e) perform skilful separations and distillations to reveal mixture composition, but beware that violent methods (strong heat, crude agents) can create artifacts and new qualities not originally present; (f) perform quantitative measures (tables of weight, density ratios) to compare bodies; (g) construct controlled experiments such as converting a measured liquid to vapor to estimate expansion (example: spirits of wine experiment showing ~100× expansion). The rubric emphasizes careful design to avoid confounding effects introduced by the method itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instances indicating continued process or series
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances devised to make visible the ongoing succession or gradual process that is usually only observed at its termination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use careful, often time-resolved observations and experiments that reveal beginnings and intermediate stages (e.g., early rudiments of life, animalculae from putrefaction, eggs and first beginnings). These instances help infer how a process proceeds step by step rather than only its end-state. Conditions for observing such processes are noted (e.g., mild heat and pliant material favor formation of life-like structures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Instances that supply the absolute wants of the senses
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances (instruments or contrivances) that fill gaps where the senses lack any access to certain kinds of information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop devices or methods that create a sensory handle on otherwise inaccessible phenomena (e.g., novel instruments beyond simple magnifiers or measures). The text indicates this is the fourth class of 'lamp' instances — seek or invent artifices that render the absolutely unperceivable perceivable; specific examples are not fully elaborated in this chunk but the principle directs experimental invention to meet sensory lacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instances that excite attention and limit subtilty
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances aimed at focusing observation and preventing over-refined speculation that outruns the senses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design instances that draw the investigator’s attention to salient, observable effects and that set practical limits on overly subtle theorizing. They serve as the fifth class of 'lamp' instances: provoke empirical observation while restraining speculative finesse that lacks sensory grounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative measurement and tables of weights (use of weight/density tables)
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematic quantitative measurement (tables of weights/densities) as a methodological instance to reveal relations among tangible bodies and to expose limits of natural variation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compile accurate tables of weights and sizes for metals, minerals, liquids, oils, and many natural and artificial bodies to reveal unexpected results (e.g., observed range of compact tangible bodies roughly within 1:21 ratio). Use careful weighing and controlled experiments (example: converting a measured quantity of spirit of wine to vapor in a bladder gave ~100× expansion) to derive proportions between tangible and aëriform states. Quantitative tables assist both theory and practice and should be used widely to test hypotheses about matter, density, and relative quantities. Ensure experimental controls to avoid artifact from procedure.
